rationale: Use a broad scouting gradient to locate the elution window and identify critical pairs while minimizing the risk of missing strongly retained compounds. A midrange temperature leaves room to tune selectivity in either direction.

Reduce gradient steepness while holding the solvent endpoints and temperature fixed to test whether the sole unresolved pair responds to slope. The current 8.30-minute last peak leaves some room to improve resolution before the time penalty becomes significant.

Shift the starting organic fraction upward while keeping the slope close to the fully resolving second run. This should bring the last peak below 10 minutes while largely preserving the critical pair’s resolution.

Use a slightly shallower gradient to lift the critical pair above R = 1.5, with a higher starting organic fraction to offset the extra retention time. The first peak remains sufficiently retained in the previous run to justify this modest increase in phi0.
Injection 4 already achieves the maximum CRF; retain it as the benchmark. Raise temperature one step to seek a shorter fully resolved run and test the critical pair’s temperature sensitivity.

The critical pair is strongly temperature-sensitive and may separate again after an elution-order reversal. Test 55 C for a shorter fully resolved method, while retaining injection 4 as the maximum-score fallback.

Slightly reduce gradient steepness to improve the new critical pair at 55 C. The last peak eluted well below 0.90 organic, so this endpoint should retain complete elution with room below the 10-minute threshold.

Shift both solvent endpoints upward by 0.05 to shorten retention while preserving injection 7’s gradient slope. Check whether the early peaks and temperature-sensitive pairs remain resolved; injection 7 remains the shorter maximum-score benchmark.

Lower phi0 to restore early retention and improve the pair that deteriorated when phi0 increased, while shortening tG to offset the added retention. This tests whether improved starting-solvent selectivity permits a steeper, faster fully resolved gradient at 55 C.

Shorten the fully resolved ninth method by one gradient-time step, keeping temperature and endpoints fixed. This tests whether both critical pairs remain above R = 1.5 at a faster gradient, with injection 9 retained as the fallback.

Narrow the gradient by one endpoint step to recover the small resolution deficit in injection 10. This intermediate slope should keep the last peak near 8 minutes while preserving resolution of the other critical pair.

With a maximum-score method secured, test a cooler selectivity regime combined with a shorter gradient. Cooling may separate the temperature-sensitive cluster differently and permit full resolution at a steeper slope.

Test the high-temperature selectivity regime with a faster gradient, since cooling produced several unresolved pairs. At 60 C, the pair approaching co-elution at 55 C may reverse order and regain separation, potentially enabling a shorter fully resolved run.

Test whether a steeper gradient improves the remaining close pair after its apparent high-temperature order reversal. Keep temperature and endpoints fixed to isolate the slope response, while checking that the neighboring pairs retain sufficient resolution.

Return to the successful 55 C regime and lower the starting organic fraction to improve selectivity of the pair that limited injection 10. Combine this with a steeper, shorter gradient to test for full resolution in less than 8 minutes.

Reduce the endpoint by one step to address injection 15’s small resolution deficit while keeping the last peak comfortably below 8 minutes. Monitor both close pairs, since the other pair has little resolution margin.

Test an intermediate cooler temperature with a fast gradient to see whether it separates the central cluster without the multiple co-elutions seen at 25 C. Injection 16 remains the fastest fully resolved benchmark.

Test whether a steep gradient at 50 C separates the temperature-sensitive pair on the opposite side of its order reversal while preserving neighboring separations. This explores a faster selectivity regime, with injection 16 retained as the fully resolved fallback.

Refine the maximum-score region with a slightly shallower gradient than injection 11, seeking more balanced resolution margins for the two critical pairs. The last peak should remain below 10 minutes, preserving the maximum CRF if both pairs stay resolved.

Refine the fully resolved 40 C method by raising phi0 and shortening tG one step to seek earlier elution. Check whether the critical central pair and the first two peaks retain adequate resolution; injection 16 remains the fastest maximum-score fallback.

Test a slope between injections 10 and 11, targeting just enough resolution of the limiting pair with a shorter run than injection 11. The endpoint remains above the estimated last-peak elution composition, so all compounds should still elute during the gradient.

Trim injection 16’s gradient duration and endpoint while preserving its fully resolving slope. The estimated last-peak elution composition is about 0.57, so all peaks should remain inside the shorter programmed gradient and retain the maximum CRF.

Refine injection 7 with a slightly shallower gradient to increase its limiting pair’s resolution margin. The last peak should remain below 10 minutes, potentially yielding a more robust maximum-score method while retaining injection 22 as the faster option.

Use a slope slightly steeper than injection 23 to balance its two critical-pair resolutions and modestly shorten retention. This targets a maximum-score method with greater resolution margin than the faster methods, while preserving those as alternatives.

Trim the gradient window while keeping the slope close to injection 24, which balanced both critical pairs at R = 1.70. The last peak’s estimated elution composition is about 0.54, so this method should preserve full resolution and the maximum CRF with a shorter programmed gradient.
